items.title: Ecosystem, Energy Flow & Ecological Pyramids
items.body:
## Ecosystem structure

- An **ecosystem** is a functional unit where **biotic** (producers, consumers, decomposers) and **abiotic** (light, water, soil, temperature) components interact.
- **Producers (autotrophs)** fix solar energy; **consumers (heterotrophs)** are primary (herbivores), secondary, tertiary; **decomposers** recycle nutrients.

## Food chains, webs & trophic levels

- Energy moves through **trophic levels** along a **food chain**; interconnected chains form a **food web** (more stable).
- **Grazing food chain** starts with green plants; **detritus food chain** starts with dead organic matter.

## Energy flow — the 10% law

- Energy flow is **unidirectional**; per **Lindeman's 10% law** only ~10% of energy passes to the next trophic level (rest lost as heat/respiration).
- Explains why food chains rarely exceed **4–5 links**.

## Ecological pyramids

| Pyramid | Usually | Can invert? |
|---|---|---|
| Number | Upright | Yes (tree ecosystem, parasites) |
| Biomass | Upright | Yes (inverted in aquatic/pond) |
| Energy | Always upright | Never (10% law) |
keyPoints: Ecosystem = biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers) + abiotic components interacting as a functional unit.
Energy flow is unidirectional; Lindeman's 10% law passes only ~10% of energy to the next trophic level.
Grazing food chain starts with green plants; detritus food chain starts with dead organic matter.
Pyramid of energy is ALWAYS upright; pyramids of number and biomass can be inverted.
Food chains rarely exceed 4-5 trophic links because of energy loss.
items.source: NCERT Environmental Studies (ecology) EXT keec chapters; standard ecology

items.title: Biodiversity, Hotspots & India's Megadiversity
items.body:
## Levels of biodiversity

- **Genetic** (variation within a species), **species** (variety of species), and **ecosystem** (variety of habitats) diversity.

## India — a megadiverse nation

- India is **one of 17 megadiverse countries**: with **~2.4% of world land area** it holds about **8% of recorded global biodiversity**.

## Biodiversity hotspots (Myers criteria)

- A hotspot must have **≥1,500 endemic vascular plant species** AND have **lost ≥70% of its primary vegetation**.
- **Four hotspots touch India:**

| Hotspot | Coverage in India |
|---|---|
| Himalaya | Entire Indian Himalayan region |
| Western Ghats & Sri Lanka | Western coastal ranges |
| Indo-Burma | North-East India (excl. Ghats) |
| Sundaland (Nicobar) | Nicobar Islands |
keyPoints: Three levels of biodiversity: genetic, species and ecosystem.
India is one of 17 megadiverse countries; ~2.4% land area holds ~8% of global recorded biodiversity.
A biodiversity hotspot needs >=1,500 endemic plant species AND >=70% loss of primary vegetation (Myers).
Four hotspots touch India: Himalaya, Western Ghats & Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and Sundaland (Nicobar).
Western Ghats and North-East (Indo-Burma) are the most biodiverse Indian regions.
items.source: MoEFCC; Conservation International hotspot criteria; NCERT ecology

items.title: Environmental Legal Framework of India
items.body:
## Key statutes

| Act | Year | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Wildlife (Protection) Act | 1972 | Protected areas & species schedules |
| Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Act | 1974 | Created CPCB/SPCBs |
| Forest (Conservation) Act | 1980 | Curbs diversion of forest land |
| Air (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Act | 1981 | Air pollution control |
| Environment (Protection) Act | 1986 | **Umbrella** act post-Bhopal |
| Biological Diversity Act | 2002 | NBA, SBBs, BMCs |
| National Green Tribunal Act | 2010 | Green court |

## Notable points

- **EPA 1986** was enacted after the **Bhopal gas tragedy (1984)** and gives effect to the **Stockholm Conference 1972**; it is the umbrella law empowering EIA notifications.
- **WPA 1972** amended in **2022** to reduce schedules to **four** (Sch. I & II = animals with graded protection; III = plants; IV = CITES-listed specimens).
- **Forest (Conservation) Act 1980** renamed **Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam** by the **2023 amendment**.
- **Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act 2023** eased compliance for AYUSH/traded users; **National Biodiversity Authority** sits at **Chennai**.
- **NGT (2010)** delivers environmental justice within timelines; principal bench at **New Delhi**.
keyPoints: EPA 1986 is the umbrella environmental law, enacted after the 1984 Bhopal tragedy and giving effect to Stockholm 1972.
Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 was amended in 2022 to just four schedules.
Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 was renamed Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam by the 2023 amendment.
Biological Diversity Act 2002 created the National Biodiversity Authority (Chennai), SBBs and BMCs; amended 2023.
Water Act (1974) created CPCB/SPCBs; NGT Act 2010 established the National Green Tribunal (principal bench, Delhi).

items.title: Protected Areas & Wildlife Conservation
items.body:
## Four categories (WPA 1972)

- **National Park** — highest protection; **no rights, no grazing** allowed.
- **Wildlife Sanctuary** — certain **regulated rights** may be permitted.
- **Conservation Reserve** — govt-owned land adjacent to NP/WLS (community-govt managed).
- **Community Reserve** — private/community land where communities volunteer to conserve.
- Network (2024): **~668 PAs** — ~102 NPs, ~515 WLS, ~47 conservation & ~4 community reserves (~4.9% of area).

## Species projects

| Project | Year | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Project Tiger | 1973 | NTCA (2005) |
| Project Elephant | 1992 | Project Elephant / MoEFCC |
| Project Cheetah | 2022 | Kuno NP (MP), African cheetahs |

- **Tiger reserves = 58** (2025); wild tiger population **3,682** (2022 census, ~70% of world's).
- **ISFR 2023**: forest cover **21.76%**, forest **+ tree cover 25.17%** of India; mangroves **4,991.68 km²** (West Bengal largest).
keyPoints: National Park allows no rights/grazing; a sanctuary may permit regulated rights (key WPA distinction).
Conservation reserves are govt land near PAs; community reserves are private/community conserved land.
Project Tiger began 1973; NTCA created 2005; India has 58 tiger reserves (2025) with 3,682 tigers (2022).
Project Elephant 1992; Project Cheetah 2022 reintroduced African cheetahs at Kuno NP, Madhya Pradesh.
ISFR 2023: forest cover 21.76% and forest+tree cover 25.17% of geographical area; mangroves 4,991.68 km2 (WB largest, the Sundarbans).

items.title: Andhra Pradesh — Protected Areas & Wetlands
items.body:
## AP national parks & tiger reserve

| PA | Type | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Papikonda | National Park | On the Godavari, Eastern Ghats |
| Sri Venkateswara | National Park | Tirupati/Seshachalam hills |
| Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam | Tiger Reserve | **Largest tiger reserve in India** (Nallamala hills; shared with Telangana) |

## AP wildlife sanctuaries & wetlands

- **Coringa WLS** — **second-largest mangrove** area in India (Godavari estuary, Kakinada).
- **Pulicat Lake** — India's **second-largest brackish-water lagoon** (after Chilika), shared with Tamil Nadu; **Nelapattu** is a key pelican breeding sanctuary nearby.
- **Kolleru Lake** — largest freshwater lake in India; **AP's only Ramsar site** (2002).
- **Rollapadu WLS** — habitat of the **Great Indian Bustard**.
- **Seshachalam** — AP's **biosphere reserve** (2010), red-sanders forest.
keyPoints: Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve is the LARGEST tiger reserve in India (Nallamala hills), shared with Telangana.
Coringa WLS (Godavari estuary) is India's second-largest mangrove formation after the Sundarbans.
Pulicat Lake is India's second-largest brackish-water lagoon (after Chilika), on the AP-Tamil Nadu border.
Kolleru Lake is AP's only Ramsar site (designated 2002); Papikonda and Sri Venkateswara are AP national parks.
Seshachalam (2010) is AP's biosphere reserve; Rollapadu WLS protects the Great Indian Bustard.

items.title: Wetlands, Biosphere Reserves & Species Conventions
items.body:
## Ramsar Convention

- **Ramsar Convention on Wetlands (1971, Ramsar, Iran)** — intergovernmental treaty for wetland conservation and 'wise use'.
- India joined in **1982**; now has **99 Ramsar sites** (as on 21.04.2026) — most in **Tamil Nadu**.
- **Montreux Record** lists Ramsar sites facing ecological change (India: Keoladeo & Loktak).

## Biosphere reserves & MAB

- Designated under **UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme (1971)**; zoned into **core, buffer, transition**.
- India has **18 biosphere reserves**; **Nilgiri (1986)** was the first; **12** are on the **World Network (WNBR)**. AP's is **Seshachalam (2010)**.

## Species/trade conventions

| Body | Focus |
|---|---|
| IUCN Red List | Global conservation status (CR/EN/VU...) |
| CITES (1973) | Trade in endangered species (Appendices I-III) |
| CMS / Bonn (1979) | Migratory species; India hosted **COP13 (Gandhinagar 2020)** |
| CBD (1992, Rio) | Biodiversity; **Nagoya** & **Cartagena** protocols |
keyPoints: Ramsar Convention on Wetlands was signed in 1971 at Ramsar, Iran; India joined in 1982 and has 99 sites (2026).
Tamil Nadu has the most Ramsar sites in India; the Montreux Record flags threatened sites (Keoladeo, Loktak).
Biosphere reserves follow UNESCO MAB (1971) with core/buffer/transition zones; India has 18, Nilgiri (1986) first.
Seshachalam (2010) is AP's biosphere reserve; 12 Indian reserves are on the UNESCO World Network (WNBR).
CITES (1973) regulates trade; CMS/Bonn (1979) covers migratory species (India hosted CMS COP13, Gandhinagar 2020); CBD (Rio 1992) has the Cartagena and Nagoya protocols.

items.title: Climate Change & the International Framework
items.body:
## The science

- **Greenhouse gases** — CO2, CH4, N2O, water vapour, O3, CFCs, and **SF6** (highest GWP). GHGs trap outgoing infrared → **global warming**.
- **IPCC** (WMO + UNEP, 1988) assesses climate science; **Sixth Assessment Report (AR6, 2021-23)** warns warming likely crosses **1.5°C** in the near term.

## Treaty timeline

| Instrument | Year | Feature |
|---|---|---|
| UNFCCC | 1992 (Rio) | Parent framework; 'common but differentiated responsibilities' |
| Kyoto Protocol | 1997 | Binding targets on developed nations; market mechanisms |
| Paris Agreement | 2015 (COP21) | Hold warming **well below 2°C**, pursue **1.5°C**; **NDCs**; net-zero goals |

## Recent COPs

- **COP27 (2022, Sharm el-Sheikh)** — created the **Loss and Damage Fund**.
- **COP28 (2023, Dubai)** — first **Global Stocktake**; called to 'transition away from fossil fuels'.
- **COP29 (2024, Baku)** — new climate-finance goal (NCQG).
- **COP30 (Nov 2025, Belem, Brazil)** — in the Amazon, focus on implementation & forests.
keyPoints: Main GHGs: CO2, CH4, N2O, water vapour, ozone, CFCs and SF6 (highest global-warming potential).
IPCC (WMO+UNEP, 1988) AR6 (2021-23) warns warming will likely cross 1.5 C in the near term.
UNFCCC (Rio 1992) is the parent treaty; Kyoto Protocol (1997) set binding targets on developed nations.
Paris Agreement (2015, COP21) aims to hold warming well below 2 C (pursue 1.5 C) via nationally determined contributions (NDCs).
Loss and Damage Fund was agreed at COP27 (2022); COP28 (2023) held the first Global Stocktake; COP30 was held at Belem, Brazil (Nov 2025).

items.title: India's Climate Action, NAPCC & Pollution Control
items.body:
## Panchamrit & net-zero (COP26, 2021)

- **500 GW** non-fossil capacity by 2030; **50%** energy from renewables by 2030; cut **1 billion tonnes** of CO2 by 2030; reduce **emissions intensity of GDP by 45%** by 2030; **net-zero by 2070**.

## NAPCC (2008) — 8 national missions

1. National **Solar** Mission 2. Enhanced **Energy Efficiency** 3. **Sustainable Habitat** 4. **Water** Mission 5. Sustaining the **Himalayan Ecosystem** 6. **Green India** Mission 7. **Sustainable Agriculture** 8. **Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change**.
- States prepare **SAPCCs** (State Action Plans).

## Mission LiFE & global initiatives

- **Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment)** — India-led, launched 2022, promotes mindful, pro-planet individual behaviour ('P3 — Pro Planet People').
- **International Solar Alliance (ISA)** and **Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI)** — both India-initiated.

## Pollution & disaster management

- **NCAP (2019)** targets particulate reduction across cities (measured via **AQI**, 6 bands).
- **Single-Use Plastic ban** from **1 July 2022**; **E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022**.
- **Disaster Management Act 2005** → **NDMA** (chaired by PM), SDMAs, **NDRF**; India follows the **Sendai Framework (2015-30)** — vital for AP's cyclone-prone coast.
keyPoints: Panchamrit (COP26, 2021): 500 GW non-fossil by 2030, 50% renewables, cut 1 bn t CO2, -45% emissions intensity, net-zero by 2070.
NAPCC (2008) has eight missions incl. Solar, Energy Efficiency, Green India, Water and Himalayan Ecosystem; states have SAPCCs.
Mission LiFE (2022) is India's pro-planet lifestyle initiative; ISA and CDRI are India-initiated global coalitions.
National Clean Air Programme (2019) uses AQI (6 bands); single-use plastic banned from 1 July 2022.
Disaster Management Act 2005 created NDMA (chaired by PM) and NDRF; India follows the Sendai Framework 2015-30.

items.title: Pollution, Climate Concepts & Ecology — Exam Fact Cluster
items.body:
## Climate-intervention concepts

- **Geoengineering (Solar Radiation Management):** injecting **sulphate aerosols** into the stratosphere and **cirrus-cloud thinning** are proposed to **reduce global warming** by reflecting/letting out heat.
- **Carbon fertilization** = **increased plant growth due to higher atmospheric CO₂**.
- **Remote sensing** can measure **chlorophyll content of vegetation, GHG emissions from rice paddies, and land-surface temperature**.
- **Neem-coated urea** is promoted because it **slows the rate of dissolution of urea in soil**, raising nitrogen-use efficiency and curbing diversion.

## Pollution chemistry

| Phenomenon | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Acid rain** | **SO₂ + NOx** → sulphuric & nitric acid |
| **Photochemical smog** | **NOx + VOCs + sunlight (UV)** → ozone (O₃) & **PAN** (peroxyacetyl nitrate) |
| **Eutrophication** | Nutrient (N, P) enrichment of water |

- **Excess nitrogenous fertilizer** → **increased soil acidity** and **nitrate leaching into groundwater** (it does **not** promote N-fixing microbes).
- **Benzene** exposure comes from automobile exhaust, tobacco smoke, wood burning, varnished furniture and polyurethane products (a VOC).
- **Bisphenol A (BPA)** is a key component of **polycarbonate** plastics and is an **endocrine disruptor**.

## Ecology essentials

- **Decomposers** are **fungi and bacteria** (viruses are NOT decomposers).
- **Symbiosis/mutualism**: coral–zooxanthellae, lichen (fungi+algae), gut protozoa, *Rhizobium*–legume.
- **Classification trap:** the **sea cow (manatee/dugong)** and **sea lion** are **mammals**; the **sea horse** is a **fish**.
keyPoints: Sulphate-aerosol injection and cirrus-cloud thinning are geoengineering methods to reduce global warming.
Carbon fertilization = higher plant growth due to increased atmospheric CO2.
Remote sensing can measure chlorophyll, paddy GHG emissions and land-surface temperature.
Neem-coated urea slows urea dissolution in soil, improving nitrogen-use efficiency.
Acid rain is caused by SO2 and NOx; photochemical smog needs NOx + VOCs + sunlight, forming O3 and PAN.
Excess nitrogenous fertilizer increases soil acidity and leaches nitrate to groundwater.
BPA is a component of polycarbonate plastic and an endocrine disruptor; benzene is a VOC from exhaust/tobacco/wood.
Decomposers are fungi and bacteria (not viruses); sea cow and sea lion are mammals while sea horse is a fish.
